title: UK police sending only three officers to World Cup as U.S. refuses to pay for help
content:
Only three police officers are being sent from the United Kingdom to the United States to help support England fans at the World Cup — a 92 per cent cut on the 40 they stationed in Germany for the European Championships in 2024.

Chief constable Mark Roberts, the National Police Chiefs’ Council’s (NPCC) lead for football, has said UK police are having to fund the three officers they are sending themselves, which is a marked change from previous tournaments where host nations ordinarily foot the bill.

The U.S. is one of the three tournament co-hosts, alongside Canada and Mexico.

“The way the operation has been organised is there is a central element with the IPCC (International Police Cooperation Centre), but then each state and local policing agency is sorting out their own local operations, so it is a complicated one,” Roberts said at a media briefing on Thursday.

“We need to manage expectations. If you went to Germany, at every station and every entrance point, you would have had an English cop there working alongside the German federal and state police.

“I took the decision that we thought it was that important to have a footprint on the ground. It is financially difficult and UKFPU (United Kingdom Football Policing Unit) has just had a 10 per cent cut to its funding this year, in year, from the Home Office, so it is a challenge.”

Asked whether the White House Task Force also knocked back efforts to lobby for additional support, Roberts said: “It hasn’t even been a conversation”.

“There is no funding,” he added. “That has been pretty clear from the outset.”

A White House Task Force source, speaking on the condition of anonymity to protect relationships, said the body recommended the UKFPU’s expertise and experience be utilised, and made the required introductions for a delegation travelling to the U.S. to present to local authorities. However, those local authorities ultimately decided against offering any funding.

The UK government has also declined to offer any financial assistance to help deploy more than three officers as part of the on-the-ground unit, Roberts added.

Although two additional police officers will be stationed at the IPCC in Washington, D.C. throughout the World Cup, an operation being funded by the U.S. government, they will not be on the ground to help assist England fans with the local authorities.

The mobile delegation unit, which is being led by superintendent Gareth Parkin, will arrive in the U.S. on June 14 ahead of England’s first group-stage match against Croatia in Dallas three days later.

They have already spoken to all the relevant local police authorities and have explained how they will be approaching the tournament, although they are not going to have any policing powers on the ground and instead define their role as “cultural interpreters”.

At the media briefing, which took place in central London, it was also revealed how many England fans had bought tickets ahead of the tournament.

Roberts said 3,315 supporters from the official travel club have bought tickets for the first match against Croatia, with an additional 7,618 people claiming to be England fans buying them online.

For England’s second fixture in Boston, where they will play Ghana on June 23, there are 3,553 supporters from the official travel club going and another 10,171 have been bought online.

And for the nation’s final group-stage game against Panama in New Jersey on June 27, 3,971 official members have tickets, and a further 10,721 have bought them online.

The Football Association also has 1,000 tickets for friends and family at each group-stage fixture.
